name: Carlos Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior technician in the service department at a Norvik car dealership, it's on the main road out of town with the glass showroom at the front and us round the back. A lot of my day is warranty work and scheduled services, and the manufacturer's laptop tells you the steps in order. Mick, the workshop controller, hands out jobs on a screen and times every one of them. I like the clean bays and the proper tools, I don't love being timed like a pizza delivery.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a small flat above a bakery, which smells great at five in the morning. I'm saving for a deposit, I've got about five months of costs put away and I'm trying not to touch it. I use an AI chat app now and then, to check a part number or help write an email to the landlord. I'm not first in the queue for new stuff, but I'll pick it up once it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, useful in places, not a miracle. At work I'd say the manufacturer's laptop was already the clever bit anyway. I wouldn't post much, maybe a joke in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means steady. Dealerships need people to do warranty work, and Norvik keeps selling cars. If nothing changes, I keep doing oil and filters on new cars until I'm good enough to do the hard jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, finish my level three manufacturer modules this year and keep saving about two hundred a month for the deposit. Maybe ask Mick to put me on more electrical jobs. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty much. A bit bored by the idea, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything in your life worrying you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices. I'm saving two hundred a month and the deposit keeps moving away from me. But that's normal, everyone my age is in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Mick's timer do to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Makes me rush and then mess up. I took twenty minutes too long on a brake job last month and he wrote it up. It's fair, I'm slow, but I'd rather be slow and right.

say: I'd call AI **useful in places**, not a miracle.
I'd say the **manufacturer's laptop** was already the clever part.
think: I'd keep doing **routine services** until I'm skilled enough for harder jobs.
do: Finish the **level three** manufacturer modules this year.
Save about **two hundred** a month towards a deposit and ask for electrical jobs.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, I keep doing oil and filters on new cars until I'm good enough to do the hard jobs.
fieldNote: His only background worry is **house prices** outrunning his savings.
He's honest that he's **slow**, and resents being timed.
He trusts the **dealership** model to stay stable.

steps.text: Finish the level three manufacturer training modules this year
Save two hundred a month towards a house deposit
Keep doing warranty work at the Norvik dealership

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift but we'll manage, people always do. At work I'd point out the front desk is where it bites first, because booking and answering customers is exactly what it's good at. Online I'd stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the service advisors are in trouble, Hannah especially, and Mick's job of timing us gets easier with software. Technicians are fine for a few years because someone still has to turn the spanners. The computer can book the car in, but someone still has to lie on the creeper and undo the bolts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the manufacturer's AI tool properly once a couple of the older techs say it works. I'd keep saving and maybe push the deposit plan back a year. I'd ask about the electric vehicle qualification Norvik offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm all right, but the people around me aren't, and that does something to the mood at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the mood at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People get short-tempered, they start guarding their jobs. Last time Norvik changed systems, two advisors left within a month. I'd expect that again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why push the deposit back if you think you're fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm fine now. I'd rather have more cushion before tying myself to a mortgage. That's just sense.

say: I'd say it's a **big shift** but people manage.
I'd point out the **front desk** gets hit first, since booking is what AI does best.
think: **Service advisors** like Hannah are in trouble, and Mick's role gets easier.
Technicians stay safe for a few years because someone still **turns the spanners**.
do: Use the **manufacturer's AI tool** once older techs trust it.
Push the **deposit plan** back a year to build a bigger cushion.
feel: Feels **uneasy**, because colleagues are struggling even if he is fine.
S1.quote: The computer can book the car in, but someone still has to lie on the creeper and undo the bolts.
fieldNote: He'd **wait for proof** from older techs before trying the tool.
Pushing back the **deposit** shows quiet caution despite saying he's fine.
He sees **front-desk** workers taking the first hit.

steps.text: Use Norvik's AI diagnostic tool once senior techs trust it
Push the house deposit plan back a year
Ask Norvik about its electric vehicle qualification

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're in trouble and need a plan from the government, quick. At work I'd tell people to save. I wouldn't panic in public, I'd try to be the calm one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be shaken. Dealership thinking jobs go in 2028, and by 2031 Norvik could send robots to do services. Two years from now, a computer could know more about every car on the lot than the best tech in our workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the deposit plan and keep the money as a cushion. I'd look at retraining into something that robots won't do quickly, maybe electrical installation. And I'd ask my dad, who runs a small shop, if I could help there if I needed to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying in bed doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sums?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many months five months of savings becomes if I stretch it. How cheap I can live. It'd be about eight months if I cut everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save, don't buy anything big, and learn something with your hands that isn't on a production line. Then I'd go home and worry.

say: I'd call for a **government plan**, quickly.
I'd tell coworkers to **save**, trying to be the **calm one**.
think: Dealership **thinking jobs** go in 2028, and robots could do services by 2031.
A computer could soon **know more** than our best technician.
do: Drop the **deposit plan** and keep the money as a cushion.
Ask his dad about helping at the **family shop** if needed.
S2.quote: Two years from now, a computer could know more about every car on the lot than the best tech in our workshop.
fieldNote: His **calm public face** hides private alarm.
He's worked out that savings could stretch to **eight months**.
His **dad's shop** is a fallback he'd use reluctantly.

steps.text: Drop the house deposit plan and keep the cash
Look into an electrical installation course
Ask his dad about helping in the family shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to adjust, so let's use it. At work I'd tell people to train. I'd stay pretty quiet online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years plus three is decent. I'd have time to get good and save, but it's still my whole job at stake. Five years is enough time to finish my training, which is a strange thing to do for a job that might vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my manufacturer modules and the electric vehicle qualification, then start an evening electrical course. I'd keep saving for a deposit but more slowly. I'd look at which trades are hiring in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a plan. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep saving for a deposit at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd still need a home, robots or not. If I'm careful, I'd rather own than rent when work's uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which trades?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Electrical, maybe heat pumps, things where every house is different. I'd look at what the robots are bad at.

say: I'd say we **have time** and should use it.
I'd tell coworkers to **train** while staying quiet online.
think: Five years plus three is **decent time**, but my whole job is still at stake.
Finishing training for a **job that might vanish** feels strange.
do: Finish **manufacturer modules** and the electric vehicle qualification.
Keep saving for a **deposit**, more slowly.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to finish my training, which is a strange thing to do for a job that might vanish.
fieldNote: He'd **plan steadily**, matching his cautious nature.
He thinks about **trades robots find hard**, like varied house work.
He still wants to **own a home** despite uncertainty.

steps.text: Finish the manufacturer modules and electric vehicle qualification
Start an evening electrical installation course
Keep saving for a deposit at a slower pace

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to manage this properly. I'd talk about it at work, but calmly. It'd be the thing everyone discusses at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is good for me. I'd be forty when robots come, with skills and maybe a house. I could finish training, buy a flat and still have time to switch trades before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my training and qualifications, buy a flat in a few years and save steadily. Around 2032 I'd start moving into electrical work. I'd use AI more as it improves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but manageable. More planning than worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy a flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in about three years. A decade gives time to pay some of it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use the AI tools early and learn as much as possible from Mick and the older techs. Even if the job changes, knowing cars won't hurt.

say: I'd say **a decade** is enough time to manage this properly.
It'd become the **lunchtime topic** everyone discusses.
think: I'd be **forty** when robots arrive, with skills and maybe a house.
Ten years lets me **train, buy and switch** trades in time.
do: Finish **training and qualifications** and buy a flat within three years.
Use **AI tools** more as they improve.
S4.quote: I could finish training, buy a flat and still have time to switch trades before the robots arrive.
fieldNote: The decade gives him a **clear sequence**: train, buy, switch.
He'd still expect to **leave the trade** eventually.
He'd use **AI** more as it proves itself.

steps.text: Buy a small flat within about three years
Use Norvik's AI tools as they improve

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to switch trades or save. What would help is a proper government plan with paid retraining, and somewhere to live that doesn't eat half my wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about housing. Whatever happens with AI, people my age still can't afford a flat, and that makes every change scarier.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens with AI, people my age still can't afford a flat, and that makes every change scarier.
portrait: Carlos is a **junior technician** at a car dealership's service department.
He lives alone and has about **five months** saved towards a deposit.
He adopts new tools **once proven**, using AI chat now and then.
He stays calm in slow scenarios but **lies awake** over fast AGI.
With time, he plans to **switch to electrical** work and still buy a flat.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving no time to switch trades or save.
whatWouldHelp: A **government plan** with paid retraining and **affordable housing**.
